newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Rebel raid seen unlikely halting Sri Lanka drive.
newsitem.headline: Rebel raid seen unlikely halting Sri Lanka drive.

text.p: A daring Tamil rebel counterattack on Sri Lankan forces was costly for both sides but will not halt the military's offensive against the rebels, analysts and diplomats said on Thursday.

A military analyst said the army was likely to resume its month-old offensive on rebel-controlled areas in the north after clearing this week's battle zone near Vavuniya, some 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital, Colombo.

A Defence Ministry spokesman told Reuters on Thursday that the area attacked by the rebels had been secured by the army and that troops were consolidating further north in towns captured earlier from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).

More than 1,000 rebels attacked the military's defences at Thandikulam and Nochchimoddai, near Vavuniya, on Monday in an attempt to overrun the army's field headquarters and gun positions, the Defence Ministry has said.
But security forces held on and by Tuesday had driven the rebels back, it said.

"The rebels will keep attacking the army. They need to show they are a fighting force. But the military will reassess their rear positions and will continue with the main operation to open the road to Jaffna," the analyst said.
State radio said Deputy Defence Minister Anuruddha Ratwatte visited the scene and spoke to the defenders in an effort to raise morale.
Some 20,000 troops began the offensive against the rebels, dubbed "Operation Jaya Sikuru" or "Sure of Victory", on May 13.

The push through the brush jungles of the northern Wanni region is intended to open a key highway between Vavuniya and the Jaffna peninsula, 100 km (60 miles) further north. The troops have captured key rebel towns in the area.
The rebel counterattack was the biggest setback yet for the operation, although casualty estimates differ widely.

The Defence Ministry said late on Wednesday that army losses in the attack had risen to 97 soldiers. It put the guerrilla death toll at 210, including women, though it said only 48 rebel bodies were found.
However, the LTTE, which seek a separate homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east, said more than 300 soldiers were killed along with 50 guerrillas.
Independent confirmation of events is not possible as international media have not been allowed into the war zone.

A former Tamil rebel group now supporting the government said at least five of its members who worked alongside soldiers at Nochchimoddai were missing. The body of one member had been recovered, an official for the group said in Vavuniya.
"There are bodies still scattered here and there at Nochchimoddai, and security forces are clearing the area," he told Reuters. "The whole area is smelling like hell."
The army had rebuilt a key bridge at Nochchimoddai that the rebels had blown up. Burnt vehicles, smouldering buildings and scarred trees made the area look like a ghost town, he added.
Military officials said on Thursday that links had been re-established with forward troops who had been cut off in the attack, and that food and other supplies were reaching them.
A Tamil politician also said the setback would be temporary.

"(The army) will lay low for a little time and continue with the offensive when they are good and ready," said rebel-turned politician Douglas Devananda, head of the Eelam People's Democratic Party. "They will eventually open their road."
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the 14-year war. The LTTE say the toll is higher.
